_comment: LINEDOWN — SUSPECT / COUNTERFEIT fixture. Beat 5, the X-factor moment.
This is the broker's lot: modules presented as Micron MTC20F2085S1RC48BA1 that have been
REMARKED — the DRAM package markings were abraded and re-printed on an already-assembled
module so it would pass as the qualified incumbent part.
TEXT FIRST: all six findings below are reproducible with pure string, regex and date
comparisons against genuine-micron-MTC20F2085S1RC48BA1.json. No image embedding required.
Each finding names the exact comparison, so a text-only implementation produces the same six
results and the same reason string as the image path. Image match is the nicer visual, not the
mechanism.
ILLUSTRATIVE AND FICTIONAL: 'Pacific Rim Components Ltd.' is an invented supplier and lot
PRC-24817 is an invented lot. Nothing here describes a real company, a real lot, or real
seized material. Do not present it as a real counterfeit case.
MODULE vs DIE — state this carefully on stage: what was falsified is the MARKING on an
assembled MODULE. The DRAM die inside is of unknown and unverifiable origin, which is exactly
the problem: we cannot say what speed bin, what vendor or what grade is in there. We are not
claiming a die substitution was analysed, because nobody decapped anything. The honest claim
is narrower and stronger: the module is not the part it says it is, so none of our
qualification data applies to it.
WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE BEAT FROM BEAT 4: this candidate's MPN *is* on the QVL and *passes*
the QVL lookup. QVL answers 'was this part tested on this platform'. It cannot answer 'is
this physical module genuine'. Two orthogonal gates, two independent findings.
photoProvenance: Quality-captured images, broker warehouse floor, 2026-10-03 09:40 local

dramPackageTopMarking.surfaceFinish: visible sanding swirl, matte patch under marking, gloss mismatch against package edges

commercial.story: excess lot from a cancelled hyperscaler order

findings.detail: The 5-character package marking does not correspond to this module SKU. A re-labeller working from a generic DDR5 package rarely gets the SKU-specific FBGA code right.
findings.plain: The code printed on the chips is not the code this exact part uses.

findings.check: dramDateCode integrity and consistency with modulePcb.firstBuildDate
findings.expected: valid YYWW, not earlier than 2024-W18 (PCB rev E2 first build)
findings.observed: sub-lot A = 2341 (2023 week 41); sub-lot B = 2354 (week 54 does not exist)
findings.detail: Sub-lot A's chips are dated seven months BEFORE the circuit board they are soldered to first existed — physically impossible. Sub-lot B fails the date-code regex outright: there is no week 54.
findings.plain: The dates do not add up. One batch says the chips are older than the board they are mounted on. The other batch has a date that cannot exist.

findings.detail: Sanding swirl and a matte patch under the printing, with gloss mismatch at the package edges. This is the physical signature of remarking: the original marking was removed and a new one printed over it.
findings.plain: The original markings were sanded off and new ones printed on top. You can see the scratch marks.

findings.check: glyphProfile and characterPitchMm match genuine reference
findings.detail: Wrong typeface and 14% wider character spacing than the manufacturer's laser glyph set.
findings.plain: The lettering is the wrong font and the wrong size.

findings.check: moduleSerialNumber matches serialRegex and falls inside issuedSerialRanges; DataMatrix present
findings.expected: 8 hex chars within an issued range, plus a readable DataMatrix
findings.observed: serial 00000000 (outside every issued range), DataMatrix absent
findings.detail: No traceable serial and no 2D code, so the module cannot be tied to any manufacturing record. All 12 sampled units carried the same serial.
findings.plain: There is no serial number the manufacturer can look up, and the square tracking code is missing entirely. Every stick we checked had the same blank serial.

findings.expected: manufacturer, location, date, serial and part number all populated and consistent
findings.observed: moduleManufacturerJep106 = 0x2C (correct) but location 0x00, date 0000, serial 00000000 all blank
findings.detail: The vendor ID was copied but the assembler, date and serial bytes were never written. Those fields are programmed at module assembly, which is a step a re-labeller does not perform. The chip claims to be Micron; the module cannot say where it was built.
findings.plain: The stick's internal data chip says 'Micron' but has no record of where or when it was actually made. Those details are written at the factory, so their absence means this stick did not come off that factory's line.

verdict.confidence: high — six independent discriminators, three of them individually sufficient
verdict.disposition: Reject lot. Refer supplier to ERAI. Add Pacific Rim Components Ltd. and lot PRC-24817 to the AVL blacklist as an automatic reject. Retain sample images and this record against the program's IATF 16949 traceability file.
verdict.plain: Fake. Six separate checks all failed, and any one of three of them would have been enough on its own. Refusing this lot looks like giving up a $364,000 discount — it actually avoids about $1.07M in scrapped parts and rebuilt servers, so the decision is roughly $702,000 better.

plain: A middleman offered us thousands of the exact part we are short of, immediately, at 29% below our normal price. The markings on the chips were sanded off and reprinted. These are not the part they claim to be, and we cannot tell what is actually inside them.
